newsitem.title: UK: Europe mkts up with US but analysts wary long-term.
newsitem.headline: Europe mkts up with US but analysts wary long-term.

text.p: European financial markets were swift to take their cue from the United States on Wednesday after Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan spoke of modest inflation and moderating growth in the U.S. economy.

But economists said Europe's knee-jerk bullish reaction, while warranted in the short term, did not completely match Europe's underlying economic situation. In Europe, structural reform was still seen well behind the U.S.
"You're talking years, rather than quarters," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London.
"The Fed has implicitly recognised that the supply side of the economy has changed. The problem is in the economy here, the structural adjustment hasn't happened."

U.S. stock and bond markets soared after Greenspan said Fed policymakers were "reasonably confident" inflation would be modest this year and said the economy has seen "basic improvements" that have raised its long-term efficiency.
Greenspan said technological innovation may have improved worker productivity and created significant new profit opportunities for businesses.

Blue chip stocks rose nearly two percent on Tuesday, and the 30-year U.S. bond prices climbed more than a point and a half. Stock indices throughout Europe and Asia followed and German, French and British bond markets also jumped. UK gilt futures scored a contract high shortly after the open.
Sonja Gibbs, senior bond strategist at Nomura International in London, said structurally, Europe could be as much as 10-15 years behind the U.S.
"It's a whole spectrum of things. You need businesses to have enough confidence to make the heavy investments in productivity improvements. You need much better developed service sectors."

She said many economies were still heavily depenedent on manufacturing and agriculture, but it was in areas such as services that flexible, low-inflation job creation could be achieved. But Paul Horne, chief international economist Smith Barney in Paris, said the impression that all of Europe has not embarked on the path to low-inflation productivity is not completely accurate.
Countries such as Finland and Ireland were excellent examples of economies that had made fundamental shifts toward robust growth without stirring inflation.
Britain is in another league in terms of size, but it too has embraced U.S.-style reform and is reaping some of the rewards, analysts said.
"Then you have the other Europe, which is led by the two economic giants and their satellites. Germany and France are the ones that are not biting the entitlement bullets," Horne said.
"There is an entitlement addiction and a job protectionist framework which takes total precedence over job creation. It is Europe's big problem, and it will continue to be."
Nevertheless, with European interest rates at historically low levels and ample liquidity, markets are paying scant attention at the moment to long-term structural issues.
"The positive tone is going to continue," Gibbs said. "But I think maybe over the next several weeks, there's likely to be a growing realisation that Europe is on the upswing."
But with that upswing, she said increased interest rates and inflationary pressures would eventually follow.
"There's not necessarily this new paradigm of continued growth and low inflation (in Europe)," she said.
Europe too has lately had little signs of inflation, partly due to the various economic straitjackets imposed by Maastricht criteria for European economic and monetary union.

But with the exception of Britain, there is also little sign of vibrant growth. Germany is expected to show just 2.2-percent growth this year, according to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.
